message.content:
In Texas, tenants have a number of statutory rights designed to protect them from unfair treatment and to ensure they receive a safe, habitable living environment. Below is an overview of key tenant rights under Texas law (Texas Property Code, Chapter 91 and related statutes). This is not legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult a qualified attorney. | Category | Key Rights | Practical Implications | |----------|------------|------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep records of the unit’s condition at move‑in and move‑out.
• If the landlord fails to return the deposit or provides an inadequate statement, you can file a claim in small‑claims court. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural elements.
• Must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition. | • Report problems promptly in writing.
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease (see below). | | **Repair & Deduct / Withhold Rent** | • If the landlord fails to repair a material defect within a reasonable time after notice, you may:
 1. Repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent (up to $500).
 2. Withhold rent until repairs are made.
 3. Terminate the lease if the defect is serious. | • Document all communication and keep receipts.
• If you withhold rent, you must give the landlord a written notice and a deadline for repairs. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination of a month‑to‑month lease: 30 days’ written notice.
• For a fixed‑term lease: notice must be given before the lease expires. | • Provide notice in writing (email, certified mail, etc.) and keep proof of delivery. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter the premises without proper notice (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can sue for damages. | | **Anti‑Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes (Fair Housing Act). | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights if you suspect discrimination. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy and cannot conduct searches without a warrant or consent, except in emergencies. | • If a landlord conducts a search without consent, you may sue for invasion of privacy. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year.
• Certain terms (e.g., “no pets” clause) can be negotiated. | • Review the lease carefully before signing; negotiate any unfavorable clauses. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the legal eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, and then obtain a writ of possession.
• Eviction cannot be carried out by the landlord without a court order. | • If you receive an eviction notice, respond promptly and consider legal counsel. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas does not have statewide rent control; however, local ordinances may apply in certain cities. | • Check local city ordinances for any rent limits or tenant protections. | | **Tenant’s Right to Organize** | • Tenants can form or join tenant associations to advocate for better housing conditions. | • Associations can lobby for policy changes and provide support to members. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications with your landlord (emails, texts, letters). Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues. 2. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code, especially Chapters 91 (Residential Landlord‑Tenant Law) and 92 (Security Deposits). 3. **Use Written Notices** – Whenever you need to notify your landlord (e.g., repair requests, notice of termination), send a written notice and keep proof of delivery. 4. **Seek Legal Help Early** – If you face a dispute (e.g., withheld deposit, unlawful entry, discrimination), consult a lawyer or a tenant advocacy organization early on. 5. **File Complaints** – If you believe your landlord has violated your rights, you can file complaints with HUD, the Texas Commission on Human Rights, or the local housing authority. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Security deposit returned within 30 days? - [ ] Landlord repaired major defects? - [ ] Landlord entered without notice? - [ ] Received an eviction notice? - [ ] Discriminatory practices suspected? If you check “yes” on any of these, you may have grounds to take action. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal questions or disputes, consult a licensed attorney in Texas.
